Fujita-Pearson scale. When a tornado tears across the landscape, how do we measure its intensity? We look at the damage it leaves behind. The Enhanced Fujita scale, or EF scale, rates tornado intensity from EF0 to EF5 based on wind speed estimates derived from structural damage rather than direct wind measurements. Ted Fujita pioneered tornado research, and Don Pearson enhanced the scale to improve accuracy and account for the variations in how buildings perform. Together their scale provides a standardized framework for assessing tornado damage severity and estimating peak wind speeds in the field.

The original F scale was introduced in nineteen seventy-one. It was replaced by the Enhanced Fujita scale in two thousand seven to better reflect building performance and modern construction standards. The scale is crucial because wind speeds are inferred from damage, not measured directly. Damage surveys of trees, buildings, and structures are analyzed to estimate the wind speeds that caused them.

EF0 tornadoes bring sixty-five to eighty-five mile-per-hour winds with minor damage. EF5 storms have winds exceeding two hundred miles per hour and cause total devastation of strong structures. At EF0, branches are stripped from trees. At EF2, roof surfaces get peeled away. By EF4, frame houses are blown away entirely. EF5 brings the complete obliteration of entire communities.

The scale is ordinal—it orders damage categories as observable destruction escalates. There's an inherent uncertainty because wind speeds are inferred from damage, not measured, and because building construction variability affects how much damage occurs. EF ratings depend on the quality of damage surveys. Meteorologists, engineers, and emergency managers use this scale to understand tornado impacts and improve building codes and hazard preparation.
